_why: The index ranks cities by `r`, the number of Wikipedias with an article.
Bots mass-created stub articles for thousands of small European settlements,
so Kurów (2,795 people) scores 236 — above Miami at 202 and Delhi at 204 —
and landed in the same tier as Paris. Tier drives what the explore map shows
at world zoom, so a Polish village sat next to Rome.
Only entries with no other claim to the tier are listed. Of the 40 small
mega/major cities, 33 are national capitals, US state capitals or heritage
sites — checked against Wikidata P1376 and P1435, not by eye — and are left
exactly as they are. Troy is in that 33: 'Bronze Age settlement' with UNESCO
status, and it belongs where it is despite a population of zero.
The replacement tier is the one the entry's population implies, using the
medians the existing tiers actually have: mega 1.9M, major 420k, notable
111k, hidden 20k. Every one of these falls under 40k.
Applied by scripts/apply-index-corrections.mjs to both copies of the index.
REMOVALS are entries that are not places. Finding them automatically does
not work: Wikidata does not file 'comune of Italy' under 'human settlement',
so that test flags 1951 of the 5000. What does work is listing what a place
is called, generously, and reading the fifty-odd entries left over. Exactly
one of them was not a city.

removals.name: unification of Germany
removals.why: A historical process, not a place. Wikidata gives it a coordinate — the Hall of Mirrors at Versailles, where the empire was proclaimed — and the index generator took that for a city at 48.8054, 2.1199, in France, tier 'notable', population 0. It surfaced when it won ownership of a nearby landmark against Versailles itself, 1 km away.
